items.title: Cloud Storage Bucket Enumeration via Predictable Naming
items.prerequisites: Basic knowledge of the target organization's naming conventions (from OSINT: company name, product names, environment labels like dev/staging/prod). A bucket-enumeration wordlist tool (S3Scanner, GCPBucketBrute, or a custom script) and network access to the relevant cloud provider's storage API endpoints.
items.whatItIs: Cloud storage buckets (like AWS S3 or Azure Blob) are often named in predictable ways based on the company or product name — things like 'companyname-prod-backups' or 'companyname-dev'. That predictability lets an attacker guess likely bucket names and simply check each one to see if it exists and whether it's publicly readable, without knowing anything in advance.
items.rootCause: Buckets get named this way for internal clarity — so engineers can tell at a glance what a bucket is for. But that same clarity makes the name guessable from outside. Combined with the fact that cloud storage lets anyone check whether a given bucket name exists at all, the naming convention itself becomes the main thing standing between an attacker and finding it.
items.impact: Where a discovered bucket also has an overly permissive access policy (see the related publicly-accessible-bucket finding), successful enumeration is the direct precursor to full data exposure; even where the bucket itself is properly locked down, exposing its existence and naming pattern gives an attacker a validated target list for further attacks (credential stuffing against pattern-matched buckets, social engineering referencing internal naming conventions).
stepsToIdentify: Gather OSINT on the organization's naming conventions from job postings, GitHub repositories, public documentation, and its known domain names/product names.

Generate a candidate bucket-name wordlist combining the company/product name with common suffixes (-prod, -dev, -staging, -backup, -uploads, -logs, -assets, -public, -private, -data) and common separators (hyphen, underscore, no separator).

Run an enumeration tool (S3Scanner for AWS, GCPBucketBrute for GCP, or a manual HTTP HEAD-request loop for any provider) against the candidate list to identify which names resolve to an existing bucket.
For each existing bucket found, separately assess its access policy (public listing, public read, public write) since existence alone is only the initial identification step, not proof of exposure.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cloud storage enumeration for the target organization's known cloud accounts/domains.
Build and run the candidate-name wordlist against the relevant cloud provider's storage-existence-check endpoint.
For each bucket confirmed to exist, attempt an unauthenticated listing/read request to determine its actual access policy.

Where a bucket is found to be both enumerable and publicly accessible, escalate testing to the specific publicly-accessible-bucket finding for full impact assessment rather than treating enumeration alone as the complete finding.

Document every discovered bucket name (existing, regardless of access level) as evidence of the naming-convention predictability, distinct from the separate access-control findings for any bucket found actually exposed.

examplePayloads.label: Automated S3 bucket enumeration against a wordlist
Manual existence check via HTTP HEAD (AWS S3)
GCP bucket brute-forcing
Azure Blob container enumeration

variants: Enumeration of storage accounts/containers themselves (the parent resource) rather than just individual bucket names, relevant to Azure's storage-account naming model.
Enumeration combined with typo-squatting variants of the legitimate bucket name to catch misconfigured or forgotten copies.
mitigation: Avoid embedding the company or product name directly in bucket names; use a randomized or non-guessable identifier (a UUID-based suffix) instead, especially for any bucket that will hold sensitive data.
Apply the principle of least privilege to every bucket's access policy regardless of naming, since naming obscurity is not a substitute for correct access control.
Enable logging on storage-access APIs and monitor for high-volume existence-check/enumeration patterns against the account.

Where cloud-provider tooling allows it, restrict bucket-existence-check responses (some providers offer options to return a uniform response regardless of existence to reduce enumeration feasibility).

links: CWE-284 (Improper Access Control)

items.title: Insecure Cloud DNS Zone Takeover
items.prerequisites: DNS enumeration tools (dig, dnsx, or a subdomain-takeover-specific scanner like Subjack or can-i-take-over-xyz's fingerprint database). Access to register/claim the specific cloud resource the dangling record points to (e.g. an Azure/AWS/GitHub Pages account) if demonstrating full exploitation, which should only proceed with explicit client authorization given the account-creation step involved.
items.whatItIs: A DNS record (usually a CNAME) points to a cloud resource — a storage bucket, a hosted app, a CDN — that's since been deleted, but the DNS record itself was never removed. Since most cloud providers let anyone claim a resource name that's no longer in use, an attacker can register that exact same name, and the company's own still-live DNS record will now send visitors straight to infrastructure the attacker controls.
items.rootCause: Deleting a cloud resource and deleting the DNS record that pointed to it are two separate steps, and nothing reliably ties them together. When a team removes the resource but forgets the DNS record, that 'dangling' record quietly becomes exploitable the moment someone else is able to claim that same resource name.
items.impact: Full control over content served from what appears, to any visitor or automated system, to be the organization's own legitimate subdomain — enabling convincing phishing pages served from a trusted domain, session-cookie theft for cookies scoped to the parent domain, and bypass of domain-allowlist-based security controls (email filters, CSP policies, OAuth redirect-URI allowlists) that trust the parent domain.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate all subdomains for the target's registered domains (via certificate-transparency logs, DNS brute-forcing, or an asset inventory if available) and resolve each to identify its current CNAME/A record target.

Cross-reference each CNAME target against a known-fingerprint database of cloud-provider "resource not found"/"this app doesn't exist" error pages (Subjack, can-i-take-over-xyz maintain such lists) to identify records pointing at a currently-nonexistent resource.

For each candidate, independently verify the dangling state by directly querying the target cloud resource's own status/existence check (not just the fingerprint match) to rule out false positives from a temporarily-unavailable but still-owned resource.

Prioritize findings by the subdomain's apparent trust level (a bare marketing subdomain vs. one referenced in email SPF/DKIM, OAuth redirect URIs, or CSP allowlists) since exploitability impact varies significantly by context.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes claiming/registering the dangling cloud resource, since this step involves creating an account or resource with a cloud provider outside the client's own tenancy, which needs clear authorization and a plan for safe, prompt teardown.
Verify the DNS record is genuinely dangling (points to a resource confirmed not to exist) using the cloud provider's own status check before attempting to claim it.

Register/claim the target resource name with the relevant cloud provider using a test/throwaway account, and confirm that the organization's existing DNS record now resolves to content the tester controls.
Serve a clearly-labeled, benign proof-of-concept page (not a functional phishing page) at the claimed resource to demonstrate the takeover without creating a genuinely deployable phishing artifact.

Immediately release/delete the claimed resource once the finding is documented, and advise the client to remove the dangling DNS record without delay given how easily this could be re-claimed by an unauthorized third party in the interim.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate subdomains and resolve CNAME targets
Check for known dangling-CNAME fingerprints
Manually confirm a candidate's dangling status against the provider directly
examplePayloads.command: curl -sI https://<dangling-target>.s3.amazonaws.com/  # or the equivalent status endpoint for the specific cloud provider/service implicated

variants: Dangling record pointing at a deprovisioned PaaS app (Azure Web Apps, Heroku) versus a deprovisioned storage bucket or CDN distribution — the claiming mechanism differs by provider/service.
Dangling record referenced in an OAuth application's redirect-URI allowlist, enabling token theft via authorization-code interception rather than just simple content spoofing.
mitigation: Integrate DNS-record cleanup into the resource-decommissioning process itself (a single workflow/checklist step, or better, automated via infrastructure-as-code teardown) so the two never drift out of sync.
Periodically scan the organization's own DNS zone for dangling records pointing at nonexistent cloud resources, using the same fingerprinting approach an external attacker would use.
Where a subdomain is only needed temporarily, use a short TTL and a documented expiry/review date rather than leaving records indefinitely after the underlying resource is gone.
Restrict which subdomains are trusted in security-sensitive contexts (OAuth redirect URIs, CSP allowlists, SPF/DKIM) to only actively-maintained, monitored hostnames.

links: CWE-350 (Reliance on Reverse DNS Resolution for a Security-Critical Action)
MITRE ATT&CK T1584.001 (Compromise Infrastructure: Domains)

items.title: Insecure CI/CD Pipeline OIDC Trust Misconfiguration
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target's CI/CD pipeline configuration (a GitHub Actions workflow file, GitLab CI config, or equivalent) if performing a white-box review, or the ability to submit a workflow run from a forked/attacker-controlled repository if testing black-box from an authorized external repository. Familiarity with OIDC federated-identity trust-policy syntax for the relevant cloud provider (AWS IAM, Azure AD, GCP Workload Identity Federation).
items.whatItIs: Modern CI/CD pipelines (like GitHub Actions) authenticate to the cloud using short-lived tokens instead of permanent passwords — the cloud trusts a token based on details like which repository, branch, or workflow generated it. If those trust conditions are set too loosely — trusting any repository in the org, any branch instead of just the main one, or any workflow — an attacker who can trigger a workflow run somewhere less trusted (a fork, a random feature branch) can get a valid token and take on the same cloud access meant only for the real deployment pipeline.
items.rootCause: These trust conditions are often configured loosely, frequently copied straight from a vendor's quick-start guide that favors broad settings to make initial setup easier. Instead of locking the trust down to the exact repository, branch, and workflow file that should be allowed, it's left open much wider than the pipeline actually needs.
items.impact: An attacker who can open a pull request from a fork, push to a permissive branch, or otherwise trigger a workflow run in a context the trust policy insufficiently restricts can cause that workflow to assume the cloud role and inherit whatever permissions it grants — frequently broad deployment or infrastructure-management permissions — resulting in a full cloud-account compromise originating from what looked like an ordinary CI/CD integration.
stepsToIdentify: Review the cloud-side OIDC trust policy (the AWS IAM role's trust relationship, Azure AD federated credential, or GCP Workload Identity Federation provider/pool binding) for the exact claim conditions enforced — subject (repo/branch/workflow), audience, and issuer.
Check whether the trust policy scopes the `sub` claim down to a specific repository AND branch/ref AND workflow file, versus a broad wildcard match at the organization or repository level only.

Determine whether the CI/CD platform's workflow-trigger configuration allows execution from forks or external pull requests, since that's the most common vector for an attacker to obtain a token under a less-trusted context.

Where white-box access to the pipeline configuration isn't available, attempt (with authorization) to trigger a workflow from a fork/feature branch and inspect whether the resulting OIDC token successfully assumes the target cloud role.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes triggering CI/CD workflow runs from a forked repository or alternate branch/workflow as part of testing the trust-policy boundary.
Identify the exact cloud role the legitimate deployment workflow assumes, and the OIDC claim conditions currently configured to trust it.

Trigger a workflow run from a context the trust policy should not (in principle) trust — a fork, a non-production branch, or a differently-named workflow file that nonetheless matches the loose condition.
Within that workflow run, attempt to assume the target cloud role using the resulting OIDC token and confirm success.

Demonstrate impact via a benign, authorized action using the assumed role's permissions (listing resources, a read-only API call) rather than a destructive action, and document the exact trust-policy condition that was insufficiently restrictive.

examplePayloads.label: Inspect an AWS IAM role's OIDC trust policy for overly broad conditions
Trigger a workflow from a fork to obtain an OIDC token under a broader trust condition
examplePayloads.command: # in the forked repo's workflow YAML: use actions/github-script or aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume set to the target role ARN, then trigger via a pull_request event

examplePayloads.label: Attempt to assume the target role using the resulting OIDC token

variants: Trust policy scoped to the correct repository but not the correct branch/ref, allowing any branch (including attacker-created feature branches) to assume the role.
Trust policy scoped correctly for repository/branch but not the specific workflow filename, allowing a new, attacker-added workflow file on an already-trusted branch to assume the role.
mitigation: Scope OIDC trust-policy conditions as tightly as possible: the specific repository, the specific branch/ref (e.g. `refs/heads/main` only), and, where the platform's token claims support it, the specific workflow filename.
Disable workflow execution from forks/external pull requests for any workflow that has access to cloud-deployment secrets or federated roles.
Apply least privilege to the cloud role itself, scoping its permissions to only what the specific deployment task requires, so even a successful trust-policy bypass has bounded impact.
Periodically audit OIDC trust-policy configurations against the vendor's current hardening guidance, since default/quick-start examples are commonly broader than production best practice.

links: CWE-290 (Authentication Bypass by Spoofing)
GitHub Docs: Security hardening your deployments (OIDC)

items.title: Insecure Default VPC Configuration Left Active
items.prerequisites: Read-only access to the target cloud account's networking configuration (VPC/security-group console or CLI access) for a white-box review, or network scanning tools (nmap) if testing black-box against IP ranges known to belong to the target's default VPC.
items.whatItIs: Every new AWS account comes with a default network setup that allows all outbound traffic (and sometimes overly broad inbound access too), with subnets that are all reachable from the internet. This finding is about production systems still running directly inside that default setup instead of a properly designed, more restrictive network.
items.rootCause: The default network exists purely so a brand-new account can launch a server immediately with zero setup — it was never meant to be a production-ready security baseline. But because it works right out of the box, teams often just keep using it and never revisit their network design once things are running.
items.impact: Resources launched into the default VPC/security-group configuration have a wider network attack surface than necessary (unrestricted outbound traffic simplifies data exfiltration and command-and-control callback for any compromised instance, and historically-created default security groups have in some cases included overly permissive inbound rules), and the lack of intentional network segmentation makes it harder to contain a compromise to a single tier/service once it occurs.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate all VPCs in the account and identify which are the provider-created defaults (flagged as such in the console/CLI output) versus custom-created VPCs.
Check whether any production workload (EC2 instances, RDS databases, load balancers) is deployed into a default VPC/default security group rather than a custom, purpose-built network.
Review the default security group's rule set for unrestricted outbound access and any inbound rules beyond what's genuinely required.
Assess whether network segmentation (separate subnets/security groups for web, application, and data tiers) exists at all, or whether everything sits in one flat network regardless of VPC origin.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cloud network configuration review and, where applicable, an authorized proof-of-concept exfiltration test from a resource in the default VPC.
Identify a resource (a test instance, if none exists in production for this specific test) running within the default VPC/security group.
From that resource, attempt outbound connections to a range of ports/protocols and destinations to confirm the extent of the unrestricted egress.

Where a compromised-instance scenario is being simulated (with authorization), demonstrate an outbound callback or a simulated data-exfiltration channel to a controlled external endpoint as proof of the egress exposure's practical impact.
Document the specific resources found running in the default network configuration and the exact rules that remain overly permissive.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate default VPCs and their security groups
Inspect the default security group's rule set
Test unrestricted outbound access from within the default VPC

variants: Default VPC still present and in active use for production workloads versus present-but-unused (lower severity, but still worth flagging as a hardening opportunity given it remains a live, exploitable attack surface if ever accidentally used).
Default security group's outbound-everything rule inherited by newly-launched resources by default because no custom security group was specified at launch time.
mitigation: Delete the default VPC in every region where it isn't intentionally in use, following the cloud provider's documented process, to remove it as an accidental deployment target entirely.
Design and deploy a custom VPC with least-privilege security groups (explicit allow-lists for required ports/protocols only, no unrestricted outbound rule) for all production workloads.
Segment the network into tiers (web/application/data) with security groups that only permit the specific inter-tier traffic required.
Include default-VPC and default-security-group checks in routine cloud security posture management (CSPM) scanning to catch drift or new accounts that haven't been hardened yet.

CWE-284 (Improper Access Control)

items.title: Missing MFA Delete on Critical Storage Buckets
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target cloud storage bucket's configuration (via console or CLI, with appropriate authorization) to check versioning and MFA-delete settings. Credentials for a test IAM principal with delete permissions on the bucket, to demonstrate the deletion/overwrite impact if MFA Delete is confirmed absent.
items.whatItIs: S3 (and similar services elsewhere) has an 'MFA Delete' setting that, when turned on, requires a valid multi-factor code — not just normal permissions — before someone can permanently delete data or turn off version history. When this is left off on buckets holding important or compliance-relevant data, anyone with regular delete permissions (including someone using a stolen credential) can permanently destroy that data with no extra barrier at all.
items.rootCause: MFA Delete has to be turned on manually by the account owner, and it can only be set up via the command line using the account's root credentials plus a physical or virtual MFA device — which is enough extra hassle that it's commonly skipped, even for buckets holding backups or audit logs where deletion would be a serious problem.
items.impact: Any principal with standard delete permissions on the bucket — whether a legitimate but compromised credential, an insider with excessive access, or an attacker who obtained IAM credentials via any other vector — can permanently delete critical data (backups, compliance-relevant logs, financial records) or disable versioning to prevent recovery, with no additional authentication step standing between ordinary API access and irreversible data loss.
stepsToIdentify: Identify buckets holding critical data (backups, audit/compliance logs, financial records) as the priority scope for this check, since MFA Delete is a targeted control for high-value data rather than a universal requirement for every bucket.
Check each identified bucket's versioning and MFA-Delete status via the bucket's versioning configuration API/console.

Cross-reference which IAM principals/roles have delete permissions on the bucket, to assess how broad the population of potential (accidental or malicious) deleters is in the absence of the MFA-Delete barrier.

Review whether any other compensating control (a bucket policy explicitly denying delete actions except from a specific, tightly-controlled principal, or object-lock/legal-hold configuration) offsets the absence of MFA Delete.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes a test deletion/version-overwrite demonstration against a non-production copy or a dedicated test object within the target bucket.
Confirm the bucket's MFA-Delete status is disabled via the versioning configuration check.
Using a test IAM principal with ordinary (non-MFA-gated) delete permissions, delete a specific object version (or a dedicated test object created for this purpose) without providing any MFA code.
Confirm the deletion succeeded with no additional authentication challenge, demonstrating the absence of the MFA-Delete barrier in practice, not just in configuration.
Document the specific critical-data buckets found without MFA Delete enabled and the population of principals capable of performing an equivalent deletion.

examplePayloads.label: Check a bucket's versioning and MFA-Delete status
Attempt a test object-version deletion without MFA
Enumerate principals with delete permissions on the bucket (policy review)

variants: MFA Delete absent on a bucket that also lacks versioning entirely, meaning deletion is not just unauthenticated-by-MFA but also unrecoverable via any version-rollback mechanism.
MFA Delete absent but partially compensated for by S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on the same bucket, which independently prevents deletion regardless of MFA-Delete status.
mitigation: Enable versioning and MFA Delete on all buckets holding critical, backup, or compliance-relevant data, accepting the operational overhead of root-user/hardware-MFA-gated configuration changes as justified for this class of data.

Where MFA Delete's operational constraints are prohibitive, apply S3 Object Lock (compliance or governance mode) as an alternative or complementary control preventing deletion/overwrite for a defined retention period.
Restrict delete permissions on critical buckets to the smallest possible set of IAM principals via bucket policy, independent of whether MFA Delete is enabled, as defense in depth.
Include MFA-Delete and Object-Lock status checks in routine cloud security posture management (CSPM) scanning for all buckets tagged as holding critical/compliance data.

links: CWE-284 (Improper Access Control)
CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark (S3 bucket configuration)

items.title: Insecure Container Escape via Privileged Docker Socket Mount
items.prerequisites: A test container/pod deployed in the target environment (or an authorized equivalent test namespace) with the Docker socket mounted, matching the misconfiguration under test. Standard Docker CLI tooling accessible from within the container.
items.whatItIs: A container is set up with access to the host machine's Docker control socket — usually to let it manage other containers or run build tasks. But that socket is essentially a master key for the entire container host. Anything inside the container that can reach it can tell Docker to spin up a brand-new container with full root access to the host's file system — completely escaping the original container's supposed isolation.
items.rootCause: The Docker socket was connected to the container to satisfy a real, legitimate need (like managing containers from within a build pipeline), without recognizing that having access to that socket is the same as having root access to the entire host — there's no real boundary between 'can talk to Docker' and 'can do anything Docker can do,' including mounting the host's file system.
items.impact: Complete compromise of the underlying container host: an attacker with code execution inside the mounted-socket container can launch a new container with the host's root filesystem bind-mounted, effectively obtaining root-equivalent access to the host and, from there, to every other container and workload running on that same host.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate running containers/pods and their volume mounts, flagging any with `/var/run/docker.sock` (or the containerd/CRI-O equivalent socket) mounted from the host.
From within a flagged container, check whether the Docker CLI or a raw socket-communication tool is available (or can be installed/copied in) to interact with the mounted socket.
Confirm the socket is genuinely reachable and responsive by issuing a benign, read-only Docker command (e.g. listing running containers) through it.

Assess whether any compensating control (a security profile like AppArmor/SELinux specifically restricting socket use, or a read-only mount) meaningfully limits what can be done via the socket despite its presence.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes container-escape testing against the specific test container/pod with the mounted socket.
From within the container, confirm connectivity to the mounted Docker socket using a benign command.
Issue a command via the socket to launch a new, privileged container with the host's root filesystem (`/`) bind-mounted into it.
From within the newly-launched privileged container, confirm root-equivalent access to the host filesystem (e.g. reading a host file only root should be able to access) as proof of the escape.
Document the exact escape command sequence and the resulting host-level access achieved, then tear down any test containers created during the demonstration.

examplePayloads.label: Confirm the Docker socket is mounted and reachable from inside the container
Escape by launching a new privileged container with the host filesystem mounted
examplePayloads.command: docker -H unix:///var/run/docker.sock run -v /:/host --rm -it alpine chroot /host sh

examplePayloads.label: Confirm host-level access from within the escaped container
examplePayloads.command: cat /host/etc/shadow  # proof-of-concept read of a host file only root should access, in an authorized test only

variants: Escape via the containerd or CRI-O socket rather than the classic Docker daemon socket, relevant to Kubernetes clusters not using Docker as the container runtime directly.
Escape via an overly permissive Kubernetes hostPath volume mount pointing at the socket path, rather than a direct Docker `-v` mount in a non-orchestrated container.
mitigation: Never mount the Docker/container-runtime socket into application containers; where dynamic container orchestration is genuinely required, use a properly-scoped, non-root-equivalent API (a dedicated build-orchestration service with its own least-privilege permission model) instead.

If socket access is unavoidable for a specific, well-understood use case, isolate that workload on a dedicated, tightly-monitored host rather than a shared multi-tenant node, and apply a restrictive security profile (AppArmor/SELinux) limiting which socket operations are permitted.
Use rootless container runtimes where feasible, which eliminate the root-equivalence of socket access entirely.
Include Docker-socket-mount detection in routine container security scanning (both static manifest review and runtime admission control) to prevent this misconfiguration from reaching production.

links: CWE-269 (Improper Privilege Management)
CIS Docker Benchmark

items.title: Insecure Kubernetes Pod Security Standards (Privileged Containers Allowed)
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target Kubernetes cluster's Pod Security Standard/Pod Security Policy configuration (or the ability to submit a test pod manifest, with authorization). kubectl configured against a test namespace in the target cluster.
items.whatItIs: The Kubernetes cluster's security settings allow pods (containers) to run with full host-level privileges — things like unrestricted root access, direct access to the host's network or process list, or dangerous low-level system capabilities — instead of enforcing the stricter, safer settings that would normally block a pod like that from even starting.
items.rootCause: The cluster's security enforcement was left at its loose default, or was never explicitly locked down to the stricter setting. This commonly happens because one early workload genuinely needed elevated privileges during initial setup, and rather than granting that one exception narrowly, the whole cluster or namespace was left permissive for everything, indefinitely.
items.impact: Any workload (including one compromised via an unrelated application-layer vulnerability) that can be deployed or already runs as a privileged pod effectively has root access to the underlying node, from which it can access the host filesystem, other pods' resources, node credentials/service-account tokens, and potentially pivot to compromise the entire cluster depending on what else is reachable from the node.
stepsToIdentify: Check the Pod Security Standards enforcement level applied to each namespace (via the `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce` label) or, for clusters still using the deprecated PSP, review the bound PodSecurityPolicy objects.
Enumerate existing running pods for any already configured with `privileged: true`, `hostPID`, `hostNetwork`, or a sensitive `hostPath` mount, using kubectl.
Where authorized, attempt to submit a test pod manifest requesting `privileged: true` in a namespace believed to be permissive, and confirm whether the admission controller accepts or rejects it.

If a privileged pod is confirmed to be schedulable, assess what's reachable from the node itself (other pods' service-account tokens, the kubelet API, cloud-provider instance-metadata service) to size the realistic escalation path.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes deploying a privileged test pod into the target cluster/namespace.
Submit a test pod manifest requesting `privileged: true` and a hostPath mount of the node's root filesystem, and confirm the admission controller accepts it.
From within the running privileged test pod, mount and access the node's root filesystem to confirm host-level access.

From the node-level vantage point, attempt to locate and read other pods' mounted service-account tokens or reach the cloud-provider instance-metadata service as a demonstration of lateral-movement potential.
Document the exact admission-control gap (missing or misconfigured Pod Security Standard) and the resulting node/cluster access achieved, then delete all test pods/resources created.

examplePayloads.label: Check Pod Security Standard enforcement label on a namespace
Enumerate existing privileged pods across the cluster
Submit a test privileged pod with a hostPath mount
examplePayloads.command: kubectl apply -f privileged_test_pod.yaml  # spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged: true, hostPath volume mounting '/'

examplePayloads.label: Confirm host filesystem access from within the privileged test pod

variants: Pod granted specific dangerous capabilities (SYS_ADMIN, SYS_PTRACE, NET_ADMIN) individually rather than the blanket `privileged: true` flag, achieving similar or partial escalation depending on the specific capability.
Pod with `hostNetwork: true` allowing it to see and interact with all host network traffic and services, distinct from the filesystem/privilege-escalation angle of a fully privileged pod.
mitigation: Enforce the Restricted Pod Security Standard cluster-wide (or at minimum Baseline, with documented, narrowly-scoped exceptions for the specific workloads that genuinely require elevated privileges).
Replace any workload's reliance on `privileged: true` with the specific, minimal Linux capabilities it actually needs, granted individually rather than as a blanket privilege escalation.
Isolate any workload that must remain privileged onto dedicated, tainted nodes separate from general-purpose workloads, limiting the blast radius of a compromise.
Use policy-as-code admission controllers (OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno) to enforce and continuously audit Pod Security Standard compliance beyond the built-in labels alone.

links: CWE-269 (Improper Privilege Management)
Kubernetes Pod Security Standards documentation

items.title: Cloud Cost Anomaly Indicating Cryptomining Compromise
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target cloud account's billing/cost-explorer console or API, and, where a compromise is suspected/confirmed, access to compute/container resource inventories to identify the specific abused instance(s).
items.whatItIs: An unexplained, sustained jump in cloud spending — unusual CPU/GPU usage on servers that shouldn't need it, unexpected resources spun up in regions the company doesn't normally use, or billing charges for things nobody provisioned. Investigating usually reveals unauthorized cryptocurrency-mining software running on compromised cloud resources, rather than any real business workload.
items.rootCause: Whatever the attacker used to get in initially — a leaked credential, an exploited app bug, an over-permissioned account — was followed by them installing mining software, which is typically the fastest way to squeeze money out of stolen cloud access. This is usually spotted through the unusual billing pattern it creates, not through any single, specific technical flaw — this finding is really about whether the organization can detect and respond to that pattern, not one root cause.
items.impact: Direct, ongoing financial loss proportional to how long the mining activity continues undetected (cryptomining costs have run into hundreds of thousands of dollars in real-world incidents before detection), plus the fact that whatever initial-access vector enabled the mining deployment likely also grants the attacker broader access to sensitive data and systems beyond just compute resources — the cost anomaly is often the first visible symptom of a much larger compromise.
stepsToIdentify: Review the cloud account's cost-explorer/billing dashboard for unexplained spend spikes, particularly compute/GPU line items disproportionate to known, budgeted workloads.
Cross-reference the spend spike's timing and affected region/service against the organization's change-management records to rule out a legitimate, undocumented workload before assuming compromise.

For confirmed anomalies, identify the specific instances/containers responsible via cost-allocation tags or resource-level billing breakdowns, then inspect those resources directly for cryptomining process indicators (unusual outbound connections to known mining-pool domains/IPs, high sustained CPU utilization with no corresponding legitimate workload).

Trace back from the compromised resource to the initial-access vector (a leaked credential, an exploited public-facing vulnerability, an overly permissive IAM role) to scope the full extent of the compromise beyond just the mining activity itself.
exploitationSteps: This finding is primarily identified through billing/monitoring review rather than actively exploited by the tester; where a real, live compromise is suspected during an engagement, treat it as an incident requiring immediate escalation to the client rather than a standard test-and-report finding.

If simulating this scenario for a readiness assessment (with explicit authorization), deploy a benign, clearly-labeled CPU-intensive test workload on a designated test instance and confirm whether the client's cost-monitoring/alerting correctly flags the resulting spend anomaly within an acceptable time window.
Assess whether any automated response capability exists (e.g. an alert triggering automatic instance isolation or termination) versus purely manual, delayed human review of billing dashboards.
Document the detection latency observed and any gaps in cost-anomaly alerting coverage (e.g. certain regions/services not included in the monitored scope) as the primary deliverable for this finding.

examplePayloads.label: Review cost-explorer data for anomalous compute spend by service/region
examplePayloads.command: aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-06-01,End=2026-07-01 --granularity DAILY --metrics UnblendedCost --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE

examplePayloads.command: aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name CPUUtilization --statistics Average --period 3600 --start-time <start> --end-time <end> --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=<instance-id>

examplePayloads.label: Check for connections to known mining-pool infrastructure from a suspect instance
examplePayloads.command: netstat -antp | grep -E ':3333|:4444|:5555|:7777|:8080'  # common mining-pool stratum ports, correlate destination IPs against threat-intel feeds

variants: Cryptomining deployed via a compromised serverless/function-as-a-service resource rather than a persistent VM, producing a different billing signature (per-invocation cost spikes rather than sustained instance CPU cost).

Cryptomining deployed within a compromised container in a shared Kubernetes cluster, where the cost signature may be masked within aggregate cluster billing unless per-namespace cost allocation is in place.
mitigation: Enable and tune cloud-provider cost-anomaly-detection features (AWS Cost Anomaly Detection, Azure Cost Management anomaly alerts, GCP Cost Anomaly Detection) with alerting routed to a team that can respond promptly, not just a monthly billing review.
Apply resource quotas and budget alerts at the account/project/namespace level so an unexpected spend spike triggers an actionable alert well before it accumulates into a large loss.

Address the underlying initial-access vector as the actual security fix — the cost anomaly is a symptom; the credential leak, vulnerable application, or overly permissive IAM policy that enabled the compromise is the root cause requiring remediation.
Restrict which principals/roles can launch new compute resources or modify instance types/counts, reducing the blast radius available to a compromised credential.
