items.title: Insecure Multi-Tenant Cloud Isolation (Shared Compute Escape)
items.prerequisites: An authorized tenant/account within the target's shared multi-tenant compute environment (a shared Kubernetes cluster, a shared serverless platform, or a shared VM-hosting environment where the organization is itself a tenant of a third-party provider). Standard container/process-inspection tooling reachable from within the tenant's own workload.
items.whatItIs: Multiple customers share the same underlying cloud infrastructure — the same cluster, the same virtualization host — with isolation between them enforced only by the platform's software boundary (containers, namespaces, or a hypervisor). A gap in that boundary — an overly loose shared setting, a hypervisor bug, or a misconfigured permission rule — can let one customer's workload access or interfere with another's, even though they're not supposed to be able to see each other at all.
items.rootCause: Isolation between tenants depends entirely on that boundary mechanism working correctly — container isolation, hypervisor-level virtualization, or specific access-control rules in something like Kubernetes. Any gap in any layer of that boundary — a missing rule restricting cross-tenant traffic, a permission scoped too broadly, or an unpatched low-level platform bug — directly breaks the isolation the whole shared-infrastructure model depends on.
items.impact: A malicious or compromised co-tenant on the same shared infrastructure can access another tenant's data, workloads, or credentials without ever needing to breach that tenant's own external-facing security controls at all, since the compromise occurs at the shared-infrastructure layer beneath any tenant-specific application security — this is a particularly severe finding for any customer relying on the platform's isolation as their primary security boundary.
stepsToIdentify: From within the organization's own tenant/namespace on the shared platform, enumerate what network paths, shared kernel resources, or platform APIs are reachable, and test whether any of them expose cross-tenant scope beyond the organization's own workloads.

For a Kubernetes-based shared cluster specifically, review NetworkPolicy configuration for whether cross-namespace traffic is genuinely restricted, and review RBAC role bindings for whether any role/service-account inadvertently has visibility across tenant namespace boundaries.

Check the platform's own security-advisory history for any known hypervisor/container-runtime escape vulnerability that might affect the specific version in use, especially if a patch has been announced but not yet confirmed applied.

Where the concern is a shared serverless platform, assess whether concurrent function executions from different tenants can ever share the same underlying execution container/warm-start environment in a way that leaks state between invocations.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes attempting cross-tenant boundary testing on the shared platform — this is unusually sensitive given the platform is often operated by a third party, so authorization should ideally involve or at minimum be transparent to the platform provider, not just the immediate client.

From the organization's own authorized tenant, attempt to reach network resources, shared kernel interfaces, or platform APIs that should be scoped to other tenants, using only non-destructive, read-only probes.

Where a specific, known escape/isolation-bypass vulnerability applies to the platform's current version, attempt a controlled, minimally-invasive proof-of-concept limited strictly to the organization's own tenant boundary (never actually crossing into another real customer's tenant, given the shared, live nature of the environment).

Document any confirmed isolation gap precisely, distinguishing between a theoretical/patched vulnerability (informational) and a practically demonstrated cross-tenant reachability issue (a genuine, high-severity finding).

Given the inherently sensitive and third-party nature of this finding, escalate promptly to both the client and, where appropriate, the platform provider rather than treating it as a standard report-and-wait finding.

examplePayloads.label: Review NetworkPolicy configuration for cross-namespace traffic restriction (Kubernetes)
Review RBAC role bindings for cross-namespace scope
examplePayloads.command: kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.namespace != .metadata.namespace)'

examplePayloads.label: From within the tenant's own pod, test reachability to a network range that should belong to another tenant's namespace only

variants: Isolation gap at the Kubernetes namespace/RBAC configuration layer (a fixable, in-organization-control misconfiguration) versus a hypervisor/container-runtime-level escape vulnerability (a platform-provider responsibility to patch).
Serverless-platform warm-start container reuse across different tenants' invocations leaking residual memory/state, distinct from a network-level cross-tenant reachability issue.
mitigation: Apply strict Kubernetes NetworkPolicies denying all cross-namespace traffic by default, with narrow, explicit allow-rules only where genuinely required.
Scope RBAC roles and service accounts strictly to their own namespace, auditing for any binding that inadvertently grants cross-namespace visibility.

Where the isolation gap stems from a platform-level (hypervisor/runtime) vulnerability, escalate to the platform provider for patching and consider dedicated (non-shared) infrastructure for the most sensitive workloads in the interim.

For workloads with the highest sensitivity/compliance requirements, evaluate whether a shared multi-tenant platform is the appropriate hosting model at all, versus dedicated, single-tenant infrastructure.

items.title: Insecure Secrets Manager Access Policy (Overly Broad)
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target cloud account's secrets-management service configuration (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager) and its associated access policies. A test IAM principal with limited, unrelated permissions to confirm whether it can unexpectedly reach secrets it shouldn't.
items.whatItIs: The permissions controlling a secrets-management service (like AWS Secrets Manager or Azure Key Vault) grant read access more broadly than needed — a blanket rule covering every secret in the account instead of just the specific ones a given team actually needs, sometimes letting one team accidentally read another team's secrets stored in the same shared service.
items.rootCause: These permissions are often set up at the broadest, simplest level for convenience — granting access to 'all secrets' instead of listing out exactly which ones are needed — because setting up narrower, per-secret rules takes more upfront work and ongoing maintenance as new secrets get added. This convenience directly undoes the whole point of using a secrets service in the first place: giving each team access to only what it actually needs.
items.impact: Any principal granted the overly-broad policy — including one compromised via an entirely unrelated vulnerability in an application that only needed access to one specific secret — can read every other secret covered by the same broad grant, turning what should be a contained, single-application credential compromise into an organization-wide secrets exposure.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the access policies attached to the target's secrets-management service and identify any using a wildcard resource scope or an overly broad principal/role assignment.
For each broadly-scoped policy, map which principals/roles it applies to and what secrets each of those principals actually needs, to quantify the gap between granted and required access.

With authorization, test a specific, narrowly-purposed test principal's actual reach by attempting to retrieve a secret unrelated to its intended function, confirming whether the broad policy allows this in practice, not just in the written policy configuration.
Check for a secrets-tagging/labeling scheme that could support a more granular policy design, to assess remediation feasibility alongside the finding itself.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes testing actual secret-retrieval reach using a designated, narrowly-purposed test IAM principal.
Using the test principal's credentials, attempt to list and retrieve secrets outside its intended, documented functional scope.

Where retrieval succeeds, document exactly which unrelated secrets were reachable and validate (with a minimal, read-only check) that at least one represents a genuine, currently-live credential rather than a stale/placeholder value.
Map the full population of principals subject to the same overly-broad policy to characterize the true scope of the exposure, not just the single test principal used for the demonstration.
Document the exact policy configuration responsible and recommend the specific, narrower scope that would satisfy the legitimate functional need.

examplePayloads.label: Review a secrets-management resource policy for overly broad scope
Attempt retrieval of an unrelated secret using a narrowly-purposed test principal
Enumerate all secrets a given role can access

variants: Overly broad access granted at the secrets-management-service level (a wildcard resource ARN) versus overly broad access granted via a separately overly-permissive IAM policy attached to the consuming role, even where the secrets-service-level policy itself is properly scoped.
Legacy access grant left in place from an earlier, less mature stage of the secrets-management rollout, before per-application scoping practices were established.
mitigation: Scope every secrets-management access policy to the specific, named secret(s) a given principal genuinely needs, avoiding wildcard resource scopes entirely.

Adopt a consistent secrets-naming/tagging convention (by application/team) that supports attribute-based access policies scaling cleanly as new secrets are added, rather than requiring a policy rewrite for every new secret.
Periodically audit secrets-management access policies against actual usage patterns (via access logs) to identify and narrow any grant that's broader than what's actually being used.

Apply the same least-privilege review rigor to secrets-management policies as to any other IAM policy, since a secrets-management misconfiguration undermines the security benefit of centralizing secrets in the first place.

links: CWE-269 (Improper Privilege Management)
CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark (Secrets Manager access policy)

items.title: Insecure Serverless Function Resource Abuse (Denial of Wallet)
items.prerequisites: Network access to the target serverless function's public-facing invocation endpoint (an API Gateway URL or a direct function URL). A load-generation tool capable of sustained, high-volume invocation (a scripted loop, or a load-testing tool like hey/vegeta).
items.whatItIs: A serverless function (billed based on how often it runs and how much compute it uses) can be triggered publicly with no limit on how many times, allowing an attacker to trigger it an enormous number of times. This doesn't necessarily take the service down — the cloud might just auto-scale to handle the load — but it can drive the company's cloud bill to an unsustainable level, purely from requests that look completely legitimate.
items.rootCause: Serverless platforms are specifically built to automatically scale up to handle demand, which is great for real traffic spikes but becomes a liability with no volume-based limit or cost cap layered on top. Without a hard ceiling on how many times something can be triggered, the usual 'the service goes down' failure mode gets replaced with a purely financial one — the service stays fully available, but the bill keeps climbing.
items.impact: Sustained abuse can generate a cloud bill many multiples of the function's normal operating cost within a short window, and because the individual invocations may each be entirely legitimate-looking requests (not malformed or attack-signature traffic), traditional security monitoring focused on error rates or malicious payloads may not flag the activity until the cost impact is already substantial.
stepsToIdentify: Identify all publicly-invokable serverless functions/API Gateway endpoints in the target environment and review each for configured rate limiting, invocation quotas, or cost-based alerting.

Check whether the function's billing model (per-invocation, per-GB-second of compute) and its configured maximum concurrency/timeout create a realistic worst-case cost ceiling, or whether that ceiling is effectively unbounded given current configuration.

Review whether a budget alert or cost-anomaly-detection mechanism is in place specifically covering this function/API, independent of the general account-wide cost-monitoring already assessed in the related cryptomining-cost-anomaly finding.

Assess whether the function performs any particularly expensive operation per invocation (a large data transformation, an external paid-API call) that would amplify the per-invocation cost impact of a denial-of-wallet attempt.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes a bounded, cost-aware load-testing demonstration against the target function, and agree an explicit invocation-volume/cost ceiling with the client before starting, given the direct financial risk of this specific test.

Establish the function's baseline per-invocation cost (from its billing configuration and typical execution duration) to calculate a safe, bounded test volume that demonstrates the vulnerability without incurring a materially significant bill.

Generate a sustained, bounded burst of invocations using a load-testing tool and confirm whether the platform accepts and processes all of them without any rate-limiting response (429) or invocation-quota rejection.

Extrapolate the demonstrated per-invocation cost to a realistic sustained-attack scenario (e.g. projected cost over 24 hours at the demonstrated rate) as the primary business-impact evidence, rather than running the actual attack to that scale.
Document the absence of any rate limit/quota/circuit-breaker and the extrapolated cost-impact projection for the report.

examplePayloads.label: Establish baseline single-invocation cost and duration
Bounded load-test burst to confirm absence of rate limiting (agree volume ceiling with client first)
Check for configured usage plans/throttling on the API Gateway front-end

variants: Denial-of-wallet targeting a function that itself calls a paid third-party API per invocation, multiplying the cost-per-invocation impact well beyond the cloud platform's own compute billing alone.
Denial-of-wallet via an authenticated but insufficiently rate-limited endpoint, exploitable by any registered user rather than requiring a fully public/unauthenticated endpoint.
mitigation: Configure an API Gateway usage plan with a defined rate limit and burst quota for every publicly-invokable function endpoint, rejecting excess invocations with a 429 rather than processing them.
Set a hard concurrency limit on the function itself as a platform-level circuit-breaker, bounding the worst-case cost regardless of invocation volume.

Configure cost-anomaly alerting and, where the platform supports it, an automated response (throttling or temporary disablement) tied specifically to this function's spend, not just account-wide billing review.
For functions that call paid third-party APIs per invocation, apply an additional, tighter internal rate limit reflecting that amplified per-invocation cost specifically.

items.title: Insecure Third-Party Cloud Marketplace AMI with Backdoor
items.prerequisites: Access to the specific third-party cloud-marketplace AMI/machine image under test, deployed to an isolated, disposable test instance/account. Standard forensic/inspection tooling (file-integrity checking, network-connection monitoring, decompilation tools) to analyze the image's actual runtime behavior.
items.whatItIs: A virtual machine image bought from a cloud marketplace — rather than built by the company or the cloud provider itself — has malicious functionality deliberately built in by whoever published it: a hidden backdoor account, a secret connection back to the attacker, or code that quietly steals data or credentials from any server launched using that image.
items.rootCause: Cloud marketplaces let outside publishers list images with fairly limited checking of what's actually inside — the platform usually verifies who the publisher is and basic policy compliance, not a deep security audit of every file in the image. So launching a server from a marketplace image means implicitly trusting that specific publisher's software, with no independent check of your own.
items.impact: Any instance launched from a backdoored marketplace image is compromised from the moment it boots, potentially before the organization's own security tooling is even installed or configured on it — the backdoor operates with whatever access level the instance itself has (which can include the cloud account's own IAM role attached to the instance), providing the attacker a foothold that long-predates any of the organization's own security controls.
stepsToIdentify: Review the marketplace listing's publisher reputation, review history, and update cadence — an unmaintained image from an obscure, unverified publisher warrants more scrutiny than one from a well-established, verified vendor.

Launch the image to an isolated, disposable test instance/account with no production data or credentials attached, and monitor its outbound network connections immediately upon boot, before any organization-specific configuration is applied.
Inspect the image's installed software, running processes, and scheduled tasks/cron jobs for anything unexpected relative to the image's advertised purpose.
Check for hardcoded credentials, unexpected listening services, or SSH authorized_keys entries pre-populated with a key the organization didn't provision.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes launching and forensically inspecting the target marketplace image in an isolated test environment.
Launch the image to a disposable test instance with no sensitive data or production IAM role attached, and monitor its behavior from the very first boot.
Capture all outbound network connections during boot and normal idle operation, flagging any callback to an unexpected, non-vendor-documented destination.
Inspect installed software and configuration for backdoor indicators (unexpected user accounts, pre-populated SSH keys, unexplained scheduled tasks).

Where a backdoor indicator is confirmed, document it precisely (the specific file/account/connection) and immediately terminate the test instance, recommending the client cease using the image and audit any production instance already launched from it.

examplePayloads.label: Monitor outbound connections from a freshly-launched test instance
Check for unexpected pre-populated SSH authorized keys
Enumerate scheduled tasks/cron jobs for unexpected entries
Check for unexpected listening services

variants: Backdoor present in the image's base OS layer versus embedded specifically in a bundled application/agent the marketplace listing advertises as its main value proposition.

Malicious behavior triggered only under specific conditions (a time-delayed logic bomb, a beacon that only activates once real production traffic/data is detected) rather than being immediately observable at first boot.
mitigation: Prefer building custom images from a trusted, minimal base (the cloud provider's own official base images) over third-party marketplace images wherever the required software can reasonably be installed and configured directly.

Where a marketplace image must be used, launch it first to an isolated test environment for a forensic review (as described above) before any production deployment, and repeat this review for any image update.

Restrict the IAM role/permissions attached to any instance launched from an unverified third-party image to the absolute minimum, limiting the blast radius if the image is later found to be compromised.

Monitor production instances launched from marketplace images with the same (or greater) scrutiny as internet-facing, externally-developed software, including outbound-connection monitoring and file-integrity checking.

items.title: Missing Cloud WAF on Public-Facing Load Balancer
items.prerequisites: Network access to the target's public-facing cloud load balancer/CDN endpoint. Standard web-application-attack payloads (a basic SQL injection probe, an XSS probe) for a benign, non-destructive test of whether a WAF layer intercepts them, plus the ability to review the load balancer/CDN configuration directly if white-box access is available.
items.whatItIs: A public-facing load balancer or CDN serving the company's website has no Web Application Firewall attached at all — or has one, but it's only set to log suspicious traffic rather than actually block it — leaving the application's own code as the only real defense against common attacks like SQL injection or cross-site scripting, with nothing filtering traffic before it gets there.
items.rootCause: Setting up a WAF is a separate step beyond just standing up a load balancer or CDN, and it's often postponed or left in 'monitor only' mode during initial rollout to avoid accidentally blocking real traffic — without a later step to switch it into actual blocking mode once it's been tuned. The extra protective layer ends up either missing entirely, or present but not actually doing anything.
items.impact: The application is exposed to common, high-volume, automated web-attack traffic (injection probes, known-bad-bot scanning, credential-stuffing tooling) with no upfront filtering layer, meaning every one of those attack patterns reaches the application's own code directly, relying entirely on the application's own input validation and business logic to defend against exactly the class of attack a WAF is specifically designed to catch cheaply and generically before it ever reaches the application.
stepsToIdentify: Check the target load balancer/CDN distribution's configuration (via console/CLI, with authorization) for an attached WAF web ACL, and if present, its rule action (block vs. count-only).

Send a benign, clearly-non-destructive attack-pattern probe (a basic SQLi/XSS test string in a request parameter, not a functional exploit) and observe whether the request is blocked at the edge (a WAF-generated 403) or reaches the application layer for processing.
Where a WAF is present but in count-only mode, review its logging/monitoring dashboard (if accessible) to confirm it is indeed only logging matches rather than blocking them.

Assess whether any managed rule set (an OWASP Core Rule Set equivalent, a cloud-provider-managed rule group) is enabled at all, versus only a custom, narrowly-scoped rule set that wouldn't catch the broader class of common attacks.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes sending benign attack-pattern probe traffic against the target public-facing endpoint to test WAF presence/behavior.

Send a representative set of common attack-pattern probes (non-functional, clearly-benign versions — e.g. a SQLi test string that would trigger detection signatures without actually being a working injection against the specific application) and observe the response.

Confirm whether each probe reached the application (a normal application-generated response, possibly an application-level error) versus being intercepted at the edge (a WAF-generated block page/403).
Where a WAF is present but not blocking, document this distinctly from a complete WAF absence, since remediation (a mode change) differs from initial deployment.
Document which specific attack-pattern categories were and weren't intercepted, to give the client a concrete picture of current coverage gaps.

examplePayloads.label: Check for an attached WAF web ACL on the target distribution
Send a benign SQLi-pattern probe to test WAF interception
Send a benign XSS-pattern probe to test WAF interception

variants: WAF present and actively blocking for one distribution/endpoint (e.g. the primary marketing site) but absent or in count-only mode for a separate, equally public-facing API endpoint or secondary application.
WAF present with a managed rule set enabled but a custom exclusion rule inadvertently created during tuning that whitelists a broader-than-intended request pattern.
mitigation: Deploy a WAF (the cloud provider's native offering or a third-party equivalent) in front of every public-facing load balancer/CDN distribution, with a recognized managed rule set (an OWASP Core Rule Set equivalent) enabled as a baseline.
Transition any WAF currently running in count/log-only mode to active blocking mode once an appropriate tuning period has confirmed an acceptably low false-positive rate against legitimate traffic.

Periodically re-test WAF effectiveness with benign attack-pattern probes (as used in this identification process) as a standing check, since rule-set updates or configuration changes can silently regress coverage.
Treat the WAF as a compensating, defense-in-depth control rather than a substitute for proper input validation and secure coding practice within the application itself.

items.title: Overly Permissive IAM Policy (Wildcard Actions/Resources)
items.prerequisites: Read access to the target cloud account's IAM policies (managed and inline) attached to users, groups, and roles. AWS CLI or the equivalent for the cloud provider in use, configured with read-only IAM inspection permissions.
items.whatItIs: A cloud permissions policy grants access using a wildcard — meaning 'any action' or 'any resource' — instead of listing out the specific things a person or system actually needs to do. This usually happens for convenience during initial setup ('just make it work') and is never narrowed down later once it becomes clear what the minimum needed permissions actually are.
items.rootCause: Writing a tightly-scoped permissions policy requires knowing in advance (or figuring out through careful review) the complete, specific list of actions and resources something needs — which takes real effort. It's much easier to just grant a broad wildcard that's guaranteed to work for anything now or later. That convenience-over-precision tradeoff is, by a wide margin, the single most common reason cloud permissions end up too broad.
items.impact: Any principal (user, role, or service) holding a wildcard-action/resource policy has far more capability than its actual function requires, meaning that if that principal's credentials are ever compromised — through any vector, including one entirely unrelated to IAM itself, such as a leaked access key or an exploited application vulnerability — the resulting impact is a full or near-full compromise of the cloud account, rather than being contained to the specific, narrow blast radius a properly-scoped policy would have limited it to.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate all IAM policies (managed and inline) across users, groups, and roles in the account, flagging any with an `"Action": "*"`, broad service-wildcard action, or `"Resource": "*"` element.

For each flagged policy, use the cloud provider's access-analyzer/last-accessed-services tooling to determine what the attached principal has actually used over a representative historical period, quantifying the gap between granted and actually-used permissions.

Prioritize findings by the principal's actual reach — a wildcard policy on a rarely-used, low-privilege test account is lower severity than the same wildcard on a principal with broad network/data access or one used by an internet-facing service.

Check whether any policy combines a wildcard action with an otherwise-narrow resource scope (or vice versa), since a wildcard on only one dimension is still a significant, if smaller, over-permissioning issue relative to a policy wildcarded on both dimensions simultaneously.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes IAM policy review and, where applicable, an authorized demonstration using a principal holding one of the identified wildcard policies.
Using the flagged principal's credentials (with authorization), attempt a range of actions well outside its documented, intended function to confirm the wildcard grant permits them in practice.

Where feasible, demonstrate a concrete escalation path enabled by the wildcard — for example, a principal with `iam:*` wildcarded can typically create or modify its own or another principal's policy to grant itself full administrative access, which is worth demonstrating explicitly as the clearest illustration of the risk.
Document each wildcard policy found, the specific unused-but-granted actions confirmed via testing, and, where demonstrated, the concrete escalation path it enables.

examplePayloads.label: Search all IAM policies for wildcard action/resource elements
examplePayloads.command: aws iam list-policies --scope Local --query 'Policies[].Arn' | xargs -I{} aws iam get-policy-version --policy-arn {} --version-id $(aws iam get-policy --policy-arn {} --query 'Policy.DefaultVersionId' --output text)

examplePayloads.label: Check what a flagged principal has actually used recently (IAM Access Analyzer)
Demonstrate a self-escalation path via an iam:* wildcarded principal (authorized test only)

variants: Wildcard action combined with a narrow, specific resource ARN (lower severity — the blast radius is bounded to that resource, but the principal can still perform any action against it).
Wildcard resource combined with a narrow, specific action (e.g. `s3:GetObject` on `Resource: *`) — bounded to one action type, but across every resource of that type in the account.
mitigation: Replace every wildcard-action/resource policy with a scoped policy enumerating the specific actions and resource ARNs the principal's actual, documented function requires.

Use the cloud provider's access-analyzer/policy-generator tooling (which derives a minimal policy from a principal's actual observed usage) as the starting point for narrowing existing wildcard grants.
Establish a mandatory least-privilege review as part of the IAM-policy-creation process itself, rather than allowing wildcard grants to be created as a default "get it working" starting point.
Periodically re-run access-analyzer reviews across the account to catch policy drift and newly-introduced wildcard grants before they accumulate.

links: CWE-284 (Improper Access Control)
CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark (IAM least-privilege policy guidance)

items.title: Instance Metadata Service Credential Theft via SSRF (IMDSv1)
items.prerequisites: A cloud-hosted application with a confirmed or suspected server-side request forgery vector — any feature that fetches a URL you supply (webhook validation, link preview, remote image import, PDF rendering, document conversion). Knowledge of the target cloud provider, since each uses a different metadata address and response format. Written authorisation covering credential retrieval, because a successful test yields live production credentials.
items.whatItIs: Every major cloud platform runs a metadata service reachable only from inside an instance, at a fixed link-local address. It answers unauthenticated HTTP requests from that instance and — critically — hands out temporary credentials for the role attached to it. If the application can be made to fetch a URL on the attacker's behalf, the request originates from inside the instance, so the metadata service answers it. The SSRF stops being a curiosity about internal reachability and becomes direct theft of production cloud credentials.
items.rootCause: The metadata service authenticates by network position alone: anything able to send it an HTTP request from the instance is treated as the instance itself. That assumption held when only instance software could reach it, but an SSRF vulnerability turns any external user into an indirect sender. The original protocol (IMDSv1) requires nothing but a plain GET, which is exactly the shape of request a naive URL-fetching feature will happily make. The newer session-oriented protocol (IMDSv2) breaks this by requiring a PUT with a header first, which simple SSRF cannot produce.
items.impact: The attacker obtains the instance role's temporary credentials and can then act as that role directly against the cloud provider's API, from anywhere, with no further access to the application. Because instance roles are frequently over-scoped, this commonly grants read access to storage buckets, databases and secrets stores well beyond what the compromised application itself needed. The activity is also attributed to a legitimate role in audit logs, so it blends into normal service traffic, and the credentials remain valid until they expire on their own schedule.
stepsToIdentify: Establish whether the application is cloud-hosted and on which provider, since the metadata address and required request shape differ between them.

Identify every feature that fetches a caller-supplied URL — webhook targets, link previews, avatar import, PDF or screenshot rendering, XML/document parsers — and confirm the request originates server-side rather than in the browser.
Test whether the fetch reaches internal addresses at all by pointing it at a harmless internal or loopback address and observing the response, error text, or timing difference.
Request the metadata root path and check whether a metadata-shaped response comes back, which confirms IMDSv1 is answering plain GET requests.
If plain requests are refused, determine whether IMDSv2 is enforced (a session token is required first) or whether a network control is blocking the address, since these are very different findings.
Check whether the fetch follows redirects and how it resolves hostnames, since redirect-based and DNS-based approaches defeat naive address blocklists.
exploitationSteps: Confirm in writing that credential retrieval is authorised before proceeding, since the next step returns live production credentials rather than a proof-of-concept value.
Retrieve the role name from the metadata credentials path, and stop there first — the role name alone proves the finding without holding any secret material.
Where full proof is explicitly authorised, retrieve the credential document and verify it is valid with a single, read-only identity call that returns only who the credentials belong to.
Enumerate the role's effective permissions using read-only policy-inspection calls rather than probing by attempting real actions, so the blast radius is documented without exercising it.
Do not use the credentials to access customer data; describe what the permissions would allow instead, and record the specific over-scoped permissions as the remediation target.

Treat any retrieved credential as sensitive engagement material: store it only as long as the finding requires, note the expiry time, and ask the client to revoke the role session at the end of testing.

variants: Redirect-based reach where the supplied URL points to an attacker-controlled host that responds with a 302 to the metadata address, defeating a blocklist applied only to the original URL.
DNS rebinding where a hostname resolves to a permitted address during validation and to the metadata address at fetch time.
Container platform variants where the metadata service is reachable from a pod and grants node-level rather than pod-level credentials.
Blind exploitation where the response is never displayed, and the credential is exfiltrated by having the fetch send it to an attacker-controlled endpoint instead.
mitigation: Enforce IMDSv2 (session-token required) instance-wide and disable IMDSv1 entirely, which defeats simple SSRF because the required PUT and header cannot be produced by a naive URL fetch.
Set the metadata hop limit to 1 so containers and nested workloads cannot reach the host's metadata endpoint.
Apply a strict destination allowlist to every server-side fetch, validating after DNS resolution and after each redirect rather than only on the submitted string.
Scope instance roles to the minimum the workload actually needs, so a stolen credential grants little — this is the control that limits impact when the others fail.
Block outbound access to the link-local metadata range from application containers at the network layer where the workload has no legitimate need for it.
Alert on instance-role credentials being used from an IP address outside the cloud provider's own ranges, which is a high-signal indicator this has already happened.

items.title: IAM Privilege Escalation via Permission Chaining
items.prerequisites: Valid credentials for a low-privileged cloud principal — a developer user, a CI/CD service account, or a role obtained from another finding. Read access to policy documents (or the ability to infer permissions by attempting read-only calls). Written authorisation covering privilege escalation testing, since a successful chain results in genuinely elevated access in a live account.
items.whatItIs: This is distinct from a single over-permissive policy: each individual permission looks reasonable in isolation, but combining them produces an escalation path the reviewer never intended. Permission to create a new version of a policy, to attach a policy to yourself, to pass a role to a service, or to update a function's execution role are all defensible grants on their own — and each is also a route from low privilege to administrator. The vulnerability is the composition, which is why policy reviews that examine grants one at a time consistently miss it.
items.rootCause: Cloud IAM evaluates each permission independently and has no concept of 'this combination is equivalent to administrator'. Policies also accumulate: a permission granted for a one-off task is rarely revoked, and permissions attached to shared roles grow over time as new use cases appear. Because writing a tightly-scoped policy requires knowing the exact action list in advance, teams grant broader service-level permissions and rely on the assumption that nobody will chain them — an assumption nothing in the platform enforces.
items.impact: A compromised low-privilege credential — a leaked developer key, an over-trusted CI token, an SSRF-obtained instance role — becomes full administrative control of the cloud account. From there the attacker can read every data store, disable logging, create persistent backdoor principals, and remove the evidence of how they arrived. Because each step uses a permission the principal legitimately holds, none of the individual API calls looks anomalous, and detection depends on recognising the sequence rather than any single event.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the current principal's effective permissions using read-only policy-inspection calls, including policies inherited through group and role membership rather than only those attached directly.

Identify permissions in the known escalation categories: creating or modifying policy versions, attaching policies, passing roles to services, creating access keys for other principals, and updating the execution role of compute resources.
For each candidate, determine what it can actually reach — a role-passing permission is only dangerous in combination with permission to create or update something that will assume that role.
Map which higher-privileged roles the principal could reach, and confirm whether their trust policies would actually permit the assumption.
Run an automated IAM path-analysis tool where scope allows, then verify its findings manually, since these tools report theoretical paths that trust policies or conditions may block in practice.
Check whether service control policies or permission boundaries are in place, since they can neutralise an otherwise-valid escalation path and change the finding's severity substantially.
exploitationSteps: Confirm in writing that escalation is authorised and agree what the end state should be, since demonstrating a path means genuinely holding elevated permissions in a live account.
Demonstrate the shortest confirmed chain rather than the most elaborate, since the shortest path is the one remediation must break.
Prefer creating a clearly-labelled temporary artefact — a distinctly named policy version or role — over modifying anything the client already relies on, so cleanup is unambiguous.
Verify elevation with a read-only call that only proves the new permission level, rather than exercising it against real resources.
Record every artefact created with its exact identifier and timestamp, and remove them at the end of testing, then confirm removal with the client.
Report the specific permission combination that made the chain possible, not merely 'IAM is over-permissive' — the fix is removing one link, and the client needs to know which.

variants: Compute-based escalation where the principal cannot assume a role directly but can attach it to a function or instance it controls, then read the credentials from inside.
Policy-version escalation where the principal can create a new version of an existing policy and set it as default, rewriting its own permissions.
Trust-policy modification where the principal can edit a privileged role's trust document to add itself as an allowed assumer.
Escalation through a CI/CD pipeline, where the ability to modify a build definition grants the pipeline's much broader role.
mitigation: Apply permission boundaries to every non-administrative principal, capping the maximum privilege reachable regardless of which policies get attached later.
Treat the escalation-enabling actions as privileged: restrict policy modification, role passing, and execution-role updates to a small, separately-governed set of principals.
Constrain role-passing permissions with an explicit condition naming which roles may be passed and to which service, rather than granting the action broadly.
Run automated IAM path analysis continuously in CI rather than at audit time, so a newly-introduced escalation path is caught when the policy changes.
Review permissions in combination rather than individually, since every finding in this class is composed of grants that each looked acceptable alone.
Alert on the escalation-enabling API calls themselves — policy version creation, trust policy edits, role attachment — which are rare in normal operation and therefore high-signal.
